titre: The Test Born of a Burning Steamboat on the Niagara
accroche: In 1837, British soldiers burn an American boat. The correspondence that follows still sets the limit of self-defense today.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the night of December 29, 1837, British soldiers cross the Niagara River from Canada and attack the American steamboat Caroline, moored on the New York side at Fort Schlosser. The boat had been supplying Canadian rebels sheltering on a nearby island. The soldiers set it on fire and send it, partly ablaze, toward Niagara Falls. An American, Amos Durfee, is killed in the assault.

London justifies the operation as self-defense: in its view, the Caroline represented a continuing threat. Washington disputes this, and the affair poisons relations between the two countries for five years, until a diplomatic correspondence sets its terms.

## A sentence written to settle a principle, not just an incident

In 1841, U.S. Secretary of State Daniel Webster writes to the British minister Henry Fox that it will be for his government to show a necessity of self-defense that is, in his words, instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice of means and no moment for deliberation. He repeats the same formula the following year in his correspondence with Lord Ashburton, who was sent to settle the dispute.

The sentence no longer concerns only the Caroline. It lays down a general rule, taken up ever since as the benchmark test of anticipatory self-defense in customary international law: a state may act in advance against a threat only if that threat is so pressing that no delay, no alternative, no consultation was possible before acting. Below that threshold, the action is aggression, not defense.

The test is put to use as early as 1946: the Nuremberg tribunal relies on the same words to reject the German argument that the invasion of Norway and Denmark in 1940 was an act of anticipatory self-defense, precisely for lack of an instant and overwhelming necessity.

## A narrower rule than it looks

What the Caroline story displaces is the idea that self-defense would be judged by intent or by perceived danger. Webster's test makes it depend on a fact that can be checked after the event, the absence of any other option at the moment of acting, which makes it very hard to meet in practice. The test has become independent of the episode that produced it: it is this formula, more than the burning of a steamboat on the Niagara, that has carried across the last two centuries.

carte.punch: A boat burned in 1837 ended up setting the line between self-defense and aggression.
carte.idee: In 1837, British soldiers burn an American steamboat accused of supplying rebels. The correspondence that settles the incident sets a test still cited today: anticipatory self-defense is lawful only if the threat is instant, overwhelming, leaving no choice and no time.

quiz.question: According to the formula Daniel Webster sets in 1841, under what condition is an act of anticipatory self-defense lawful in international law?
choix: The necessity of self-defense must be instant and overwhelming, leaving no other choice and no time for deliberation
The acting state must have warned the targeted state beforehand of its intention to strike first
The perceived threat must be confirmed by a favorable vote of the United Nations Security Council
The action must be proportionate to the number of casualties caused by the initial attack it prevents
quiz.explication: Webster sets no condition of an international vote or advance warning: it is the instant and overwhelming nature of the threat, with no other option and no time to reflect, that alone makes a preventive strike lawful. Below this very narrow threshold, the action is aggression.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who is killed in the British raid on the Caroline in 1837?
choix: A British soldier, shot by the ship's crew
The captain of the Caroline, who stayed at his post
A leader of the Canadian rebels sheltering on the island
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An American, Amos Durfee, is killed in the assault by British soldiers on the steamboat moored on the New York side, at Fort Schlosser.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does the Nuremberg tribunal use the Caroline test in 1946?
choix: To convict the United Kingdom for its 1837 raid on the steamboat Caroline
To reject the German argument that the invasion of Norway was self-defense
To set a new standard specific to modern naval warfare
To recognize that the German invasion met this test
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The tribunal relies on the same words as Webster to reject the German argument, for lack of an instant and overwhelming necessity justifying the invasion of Norway and Denmark in 1940.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why do British soldiers attack the Caroline in 1837?
choix: It was carrying British troops without authorization from Canada
It was smuggling liquor across the border
It was spying on behalf of the rebels under a neutral flag
It was supplying Canadian rebels sheltering on a nearby island
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The American steamboat was supplying Canadian rebels sheltering on an island near the Niagara, which London then invokes to justify the operation as self-defense.
